                                                     Abstract
          We study low-degree testing for group-valued functions over a Boolean slice. Specifically
      given a degree parameter d and oracle access to a function f : {0, 1}nn/2 → G where {0, 1}nk
      denotes the set of vectors in {0, 1}n of Hamming weight k and G is an Abelian group (not
      necessarily finite), the low-degree testing problem asks us to distinguish the case where f is a
      polynomial of degree at most d (with coefficients from G) or is ε-far from the set of all such
      polynomials. Classical works in this area considered functions with domain Fnq and range Fq .
      More recent works have considered the setting where the domain is the Boolean cube [Bafna,
      Srinivasan, Sudan (Random Structures and Algorithms 2020), Amireddy, Srinivasan, Sudan
      (RANDOM 2023)], or when the domain is the slice (i.e., {0, 1}nk ) and the range is F2 [David,
      Dinur, Goldenberg, Kindler and Shinkar (SIAM Journal on Computing 2017), Kalai, Lifshitz,
      Minzer and Ziegler (FOCS 2024)]. Each of the changes introduces new challenges in designing
      and analyzing low-degree tests and this happens again in our setting with domain being a slice
      and range is general. Indeed the previous methods fail even when the domain is a Boolean slice
      and the range is F3 .

          Our main theorem gives a test that makes Od (1) (specifically exp(dO(1) )) queries to f and
      accepts degree-d functions while rejecting functions that are ε-far with probability Ω(ε). The
      central proof idea is to reduce this low-degree testing problem to the problem of low-degree
      testing on the cube. Specifically we show how to randomly embed the n/2-dimensional cube
      {0, 1}n/2 in the n-dimensional slice while nearly preserving the proximity of f to the space
      of degree-d polynomials on this cube (with high probability). While the embedding is simple
      and natural, the analysis involves a careful induction (seen in some prior works on low-degree

1    Introduction
The low-degree testing problem, namely the task of testing if a multivariate function given as an
oracle is (close to) a low-degree polynomial with few oracle queries, has been a fundamental problem
in theoretical computer science for over three decades. (Some of the earlier major milestones in this
line of work include [BLR93; RS96; AS98; ALMSS98; RS97; AS03; AKKLR05; KR06].) This
problem has been studied in many different settings, settings that vary depending on the domain
of the function, the range of the function, on the relationship between the degree and field/group
size, and on the coarseness/fineness of the analysis. In this work we consider this problem in yet
another new setting, where the domain is a Boolean “slice” and the range is an Abelian group. Here
a “slice” is a subset of points in the Boolean cube {0, 1}n all of the same Hamming weight — we use
{0, 1}nk to denote the k-th slice, namely points of Hamming weight k. A polynomial over a group
G has coefficients from G while the variables take on integer (in our case one of 0/1) values with
evaluation defined in the natural way. (For simplicity the reader may simply think of G as the reals
while reading this section.)
    The slice is often an important domain to understand, especially in the context of average case
analysis of algorithms. Just as the uniform distribution over {0, 1}n models a uniformly random
graph and the p-biased distribution models a graph drawn from Gn,p , the slice naturally corresponds
to a random graph drawn from G(n, m) — a graph on n vertices with exactly m edges.
    Our main motivation for studying this setting however is technical, to see what kind of tools can
be brought to bear on this problem in our setting. Indeed low-degree testing has been a great source
of connections to powerful mathematical tools, including studies of (higher order) Fourier analysis,
affine invariance, high-dimensional expansion, (global) hypercontractivity. The two directions of
prior works that come closest to our setting are from the works of David, Dinur, Goldenberg, Kindler
and Shinkar [DDGKS17] and Kalai, Lifshitz, Minzer and Ziegler [KLMZ24] who consider functions
from the slice to F2 ; and the works of Bafna, Srinivasan and Sudan [BSS20] and Amireddy, Srinivasan
and Sudan [ASS23] who consider the setting of functions from the Boolean cube to Abelian groups.
It turns out neither of these settings capture our setting adequately and indeed even a natural test
is not obvious. The latter works rely strongly on the ability to set variables independently allowing
tests of n-dimensional functions to sample points from a tensor product space. This allows them
to invoke hypercontractivity which is well analyzed in such settings. The former works [DDGKS17;
KLMZ24] roughly pick a random linear subspace of Fn2 and condition it on being in the middle slice
{0, 1}nn/2 . While this conditioning is satisfied only with inverse polynomial probability in n (for
O(1) dimensional spaces) that is still a relatively high probability event and allows them to build
dense models that are closer to Fn2 and lift the behavior of tests from there. If the range however is
R (or even F3 ), the analogous test would pick subspaces in Rn (or Fn3 ) and condition it on being in
{0, 1}nn/2 , which of course happens with zero probability (or exponentially small in n). With such
low probability occurrences it is hard to envision dense models capturing the behavior of the tests.
    Nevertheless in this work we are able to design a low-degree test for our setting. Namely given
a degree parameter d we design a test Td that makes Od (1) queries to an oracle for a function
f : {0, 1}nn/2 → G and accepts degree ⩽ d polynomials while rejecting functions that are ε-far with
probability Ωd (ε). The key ingredient in our test is to embed a copy of an n/2-dimensional cube
in the n/2-slice in n dimensions. While this embedding is quite natural, it is a priori unclear how
to analyze it, and to do so, we have to blend an inductive argument going back to an analysis of
low-degree tests due to Bhattacharyya, Kopparty, Schoenebeck, Sudan, and Zuckerman [BKSSZ10]

1.1   Our results
We show the following.
Theorem 1.1 (Low-degree test over slice). For every Abelian group G, degree parameter d ⩾
0, even integer n ⩾ 2, there exists a exp(dO(1) ) query test Tslice such that for all functions f :
{0, 1}nn/2 → G, we have

   • (Completeness) If f is degree-d, then Tslice accepts f with probability 1.

   • (Soundness) For every ε > 0, if f is ε-far from degree-d, then Tslice rejects f with probability
     Ωd (ε).
We note that the rejection probability of the above test can be made Ω(ε) by repeating the test an
appropriate Od (1) (in fact, exp(dO(1) )) number of times. Furthermore, the test Tslice of Theorem 1.1
can be easily described as follows (a more formal description is given in Section 3):
  1. Choose a perfect matching M over the complete graph on n vertices uniformly at random.

  2. Obtain oracle access to the restricted function f (M ) : {0, 1}n/2 → G defined by setting xj =
     1 − xi for all edges (i, j) of the matching M where i < j ∈ [n].

1.2      Technical contributions
A linearity test for the slice was given by [DDGKS17] (for functions from {0, 1}nk to F2 ), which
was later extended by [KLMZ24] to higher degrees (also to the more challenging “1% regime”).2
However, these tests do not seem to work when the co-domain is changed to a larger field (e.g. R)
as discussed in the introduction. We instead give a reduction from slices to Boolean grids and use
the low-degree tests over grids given by [BSS20; ASS23] (which work for any Abelian group as the
co-domain) whose analyses follow an iterative argument similar to the tests of [BKSSZ10; HSS13].
    Changing the structure of both the domain (from {0, 1}n to slices) and the co-domain (from F2
to general Abelian groups) of the functions being tested brings in several new challenges that we will

1.3    Open problems
We list a few natural questions that arise from our work.

Gluing polynomials over subdomains. The key strategy used throughout this paper and in
[BKSSZ10] can be described in the following way: Starting with some function f : D → G defined
on some domain D, we restrict to some randomly chosen subdomain Di ⊆ D, and perform a low-
degree test there, either by using an induction hypothesis on the size of the domain, or using that
Di is a simpler domain like a Boolean grid.
    Such a test only works under the condition that if f is far from being a degree-d polynomial,
then many of the restrictions are also far from being a degree-d polynomial, or conversely, if f is
close to polynomials Pi of degree-d on many domains Di , then there exists a global polynomial
P : D → G that is close to f .
    This leads us to ask the following general question:

Question 1. For an Abelian group G, a set D ⊆ Gn and a collection of subsets Di ⊆ D, when
does it hold that for any set of degree-d polynomials Qi ∈ G⩽d [x1 , . . . , xn ] with Qi ≡ Qj on Di ∩ Dj ,
there exists a polynomial Q ∈ G⩽d [x1 , . . . , xn ] satisfying Q ≡ Qi on Di . That is, when can we “glue”
degree-d polynomials defined on the subdomains Di , to a global one defined on the domain D?

    As a key step in the proof, [BKSSZ10] (raises and) answers the above question for the case when
D = Fn2 with the subsets Di being hyperplanes over F2 . Similarly, in the local testing over grids
works of [ASS23; BSS20], the domain D = {0, 1}n whereas Di are “subcubes” obtained by restricting
some variables to constants. Similarly in a related work of Dinur, Filmus and Harsha [DFH25], the
authors again use a certain agreement tester, to glue polynomials defined over restricted domains
into one global polynomial.
    In the same spirit, in this paper, we show that D = {0, 1}nn/2 with subsets being certain embed-
dings of the grid {0, 1}n/2 also has the desired structure (see Proposition 4.1 and Lemma 6.2). Our
key contribution has been finding a nice basis for the large domain D, such that the restrictions of
the basis to the subdomains Di are well-behaved. A better understanding of the general question
could lead to further progress on low-degree tests over other domains.

Efficient decoding algorithms over the slice. Our results can be stated as showing that the
code underlying low-degree evaluations over Boolean slices is locally testable. A recent work of
Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan and Sudan [ABSS25] gives tight bounds on the distance of this code.
Hence it is also natural to ask whether the same code also admits efficient decoding, local decoding,
and list-decoding algorithms.

2     Preliminaries
We start with some basic notations and definitions. Throughout the paper, we let {0, 1}nk denote
the k-th Boolean slice, i.e., elements of {0, 1}n of Hamming weight k, and let G denote an arbitrary
Abelian group. For D ⊆ {0, 1}n , we say that a function f : D → G is degree-d if it can be represented
by a polynomial of degree at most d, where in this paper, a polynomial over an Abelian group G
refers to some linear combination of multilinear monomials of degree at most d with coefficients
coming from G. We let Pd (D, G), or simply Pd (D) when G is clear from context, denote the family
of degree-d functions with domain D and co-domain G. For f, g : D → G, we denote their relative
Hamming distance by δ(f, g) := Prx∈D [f (x) ̸= g(x)]. For f : D → G and a family of functions with
domain D (with co-domain G), we also have the notation δF (f ) := minP ∈F δ(f, P ), which we refer
to as the distance of f from F. We say that f is ε-close to F if δF (f ) ⩽ ε and is ε-far otherwise.
When F is the family Pd (D) and D is clear from context, we denote δd (f ) := δPd (D) (f ). For a
domain D, a subset S ⊆ D and function f : D → G, we let f |S : S → G denote the function f
restricted to the domain S.
    For S ⊆ [n] and x ∈ {0, 1}n , we let x|S denote the restriction of the string x to the coordinates
of S and for a ∈ {0, 1}|S| , we let aS denote the assignment to the coordinates indexed by S by
identifying S with [|S|] in increasing order of the coordinates. Similarly, we let {0, 1}Sk denote the
strings in {0, 1}S of Hamming weight k. For disjoint subsets S, T ⊆ [n], and strings x ∈ {0, 1}S and
y ∈ {0, 1}T , we let x ◦ y ∈ {0, 1}S∪T denote their concatenation.
